claim: Isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) is an essential metabolic output of the apicoplast organelle in Plasmodium falciparum malaria parasites.
source: Isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) is an essential metabolic output of the apicoplast organelle in Plasmodium falciparum malaria parasites and is required for prenylation-dependent vesicular trafficking and other cellular processes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim and is supported by the broader literature context provided in the introduction.

claim: IPP is required for prenylation-dependent vesicular trafficking and other cellular processes.
source: Isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) is an essential metabolic output of the apicoplast organelle in Plasmodium falciparum malaria parasites and is required for prenylation-dependent vesicular trafficking and other cellular processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the introduction to prior work (Guggisberg et al., 2014; Jomaa et al., 1999; van Dooren et al., 2006; Simão-Gurge et al., 2019).

claim: Inhibiting IPP synthesis blocks apicoplast elongation and inheritance by daughter merozoites.
source: Inhibiting IPP synthesis blocks apicoplast elongation and inheritance by daughter merozoites, and apicoplast biogenesis is rescued by exogenous IPP and polyprenols.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2, including microscopy and genetic experiments with FOS treatment and ΔDXS parasites.

claim: Apicoplast biogenesis is rescued by exogenous IPP and polyprenols.
source: Inhibiting IPP synthesis blocks apicoplast elongation and inheritance by daughter merozoites, and apicoplast biogenesis is rescued by exogenous IPP and polyprenols.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 1, 4, and 7 showing rescue of apicoplast morphology with IPP and polyprenols.

claim: Knockout of MiaA has no effect on blood-stage parasites.
source: Knockout of the only known isoprenoid-dependent apicoplast pathway, tRNA prenylation by MiaA, has no effect on blood-stage parasites and thus cannot explain apicoplast reliance on IPP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing normal growth and apicoplast morphology in ΔMiaA parasites.

claim: MiaA-dependent tRNA prenylation cannot explain apicoplast reliance on IPP.
source: Knockout of the only known isoprenoid-dependent apicoplast pathway, tRNA prenylation by MiaA, has no effect on blood-stage parasites and thus cannot explain apicoplast reliance on IPP.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation that ΔMiaA parasites are viable with intact apicoplasts (Figure 3).

claim: An annotated polyprenyl synthase (PPS, PF3D7_0202700) localizes to the apicoplast.
source: However, we have localized an annotated polyprenyl synthase (PPS) to the apicoplast.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6 showing co-localization with apicoplast markers and N-terminal processing.

claim: PPS knockdown is lethal to parasites.
source: PPS knockdown is lethal to parasites, rescued by IPP and long- (C50) but not short-chain (≤C20) prenyl alcohols, and blocks apicoplast biogenesis, thus explaining apicoplast dependence on isoprenoid synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6E showing growth defects in -aTc conditions.

claim: PPS knockdown is rescued by IPP and long-chain (C50) but not short-chain (≤C20) prenyl alcohols.
source: PPS knockdown is lethal to parasites, rescued by IPP and long- (C50) but not short-chain (≤C20) prenyl alcohols, and blocks apicoplast biogenesis, thus explaining apicoplast dependence on isoprenoid synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6E and 7 showing selective rescue by decaprenol but not FOH or GGOH.

claim: PPS knockdown blocks apicoplast biogenesis.
source: PPS knockdown is lethal to parasites, rescued by IPP and long- (C50) but not short-chain (≤C20) prenyl alcohols, and blocks apicoplast biogenesis, thus explaining apicoplast dependence on isoprenoid synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing defects in apicoplast elongation and loss of apicoplast genome in PPS KD parasites.

claim: PPS synthesizes long-chain polyprenols critical for apicoplast membrane fluidity and biogenesis.
source: We hypothesize that PPS synthesizes long-chain polyprenols critical for apicoplast membrane fluidity and biogenesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations and is explicitly stated as speculative.

claim: The apicoplast is essential for parasite viability.
source: Plasmodium falciparum malaria parasites are single-celled eukaryotes that harbor a non-photosynthetic plastid organelle called the apicoplast which houses core metabolic pathways and is essential for parasite viability (Ralph et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Ralph et al., 2004).

claim: Many apicoplast pathways, including heme and fatty acid synthesis, are dispensable during parasite infection of erythrocytes.
source: However, cashing in on this potential has proved challenging since many apicoplast pathways, including heme (Ke et al., 2014; Goldberg and Sigala, 2017) and fatty acid synthesis (Yu et al., 2008; Shears et al., 2015), are dispensable during parasite infection of erythrocytes when all malaria symptoms arise.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Ke et al., 2014; Goldberg and Sigala, 2017; Yu et al., 2008; Shears et al., 2015).

claim: Multiple antibiotics, including doxycycline and clindamycin, block apicoplast biogenesis and inheritance and kill parasites.
source: Multiple antibiotics, including doxycycline and clindamycin, block apicoplast biogenesis and inheritance and kill parasites, but their slow activity over several lifecycles has been a fundamental limitation to broad clinical application (Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007).

claim: The apicoplast biosynthesizes and exports IPP and DMAPP via the MEP pathway.
source: A key, essential function of the apicoplast is biosynthesis and export of the isomeric isoprenoid precursors, isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP), and dimethylallyl pyrophosphate (DMAPP), via the non-mevalonate/methylerythritol phosphate (MEP) pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the broader context of the introduction.

claim: IPP and DMAPP are critical for diverse cellular processes including prenylation of proteins, dolichol-mediated protein glycosylation, and biosynthesis of mitochondrial ubiquinone and heme A.
source: IPP and DMAPP, which can be interconverted by an IPP isomerase, are critical for diverse cellular processes that include prenylation of proteins involved in vesicular trafficking, dolichol-mediated protein glycosylation, and biosynthesis of mitochondrial ubiquinone and heme A (Guggisberg et al., 2014; Jomaa et al., 1999; van Dooren et al., 2006; Simão-Gurge et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Guggisberg et al., 2014; Jomaa et al., 1999; van Dooren et al., 2006; Simão-Gurge et al., 2019).

claim: Exogenous IPP rescues parasites from lethal apicoplast dysfunction or disruption.
source: Indeed, exogenous IPP is able to rescue parasites from lethal apicoplast dysfunction or disruption, highlighting the essential requirement for this isoprenoid precursor outside the apicoplast in blood-stage parasites (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011).

claim: Fosmidomycin (FOS) kills parasites in the first lifecycle of treatment.
source: Consistent with these critical cellular roles for IPP, the MEP pathway inhibitor fosmidomycin (FOS) kills parasites in the first lifecycle of treatment (Jomaa et al., 1999; Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Uddin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Jomaa et al., 1999; Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Uddin et al., 2018).

claim: Doxycycline and clindamycin cause delayed, second-cycle death in Plasmodium parasites.
source: This first-cycle FOS activity contrasts with the delayed, second-cycle death observed for Plasmodium parasites treated with antibiotics such as doxycycline and clindamycin that are thought to block translation of the 35 kb apicoplast genome and the predominantly organelle maintenance pathways it encodes.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field as described in the introduction.

claim: Essential apicoplast functions can be segregated into anabolic pathways causing first-cycle death and housekeeping pathways causing delayed, second-cycle defects.
source: These contrasting kinetics have led to a prevailing view in the literature that essential apicoplast functions can be segregated into two general categories: (1) anabolic pathways that produce metabolites required outside the apicoplast and whose inhibition causes first-cycle parasite death and (2) housekeeping pathways that are only required for organelle maintenance and whose inhibition causes delayed, second-cycle defects (Ramya et al., 2007; Kennedy et al., 2019b; Kennedy et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is a prevailing view in the literature supported by citations (Ramya et al., 2007; Kennedy et al., 2019b; Kennedy et al., 2019a).

claim: Exceptions to the simple paradigm of apicoplast function segregation have been reported.
source: Although this simple paradigm has been useful for conceptualizing general apicoplast functions, exceptions to this model have been reported (Uddin et al., 2018; Amberg-Johnson et al., 2017; Boucher and Yeh, 2019; Okada et al., 2020) and thus its general validity remains uncertain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Uddin et al., 2018; Amberg-Johnson et al., 2017; Boucher and Yeh, 2019; Okada et al., 2020).

claim: Isoprenoid biosynthesis has been thought to only serve essential roles outside the apicoplast.
source: Since exogenous IPP rescues parasites from lethal apicoplast disruption (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011), isoprenoid biosynthesis has been thought to only serve essential roles outside this organelle (Guggisberg et al., 2014; Uddin et al., 2018; Kennedy et al., 2019a; Amberg-Johnson et al., 2017; Gisselberg et al., 2018; Imlay and Odom, 2014; Gisselberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a prevailing view in the literature supported by citations (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Guggisberg et al., 2014; Uddin et al., 2018; Kennedy et al., 2019a; Amberg-Johnson et al., 2017; Gisselberg et al., 2018; Imlay and Odom, 2014; Gisselberg et al., 2013).

claim: P. falciparum expresses an essential polyprenyl synthase (PF3D7_1128400) that localizes to the cytoplasm and other cellular foci outside the apicoplast and mitochondrion.
source: Indeed, P. falciparum expresses an essential polyprenyl synthase (PPS, PF3D7_1128400) that appears to localize to the cytoplasm and other cellular foci outside the apicoplast and mitochondrion (Gabriel et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gabriel et al., 2015a).

claim: PF3D7_1128400 has dual farnesyl/geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate synthase (FPPS/GGPPS) activity.
source: The dual farnesyl/geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate synthase (FPPS/GGPPS) activity of this protein is critical for condensing isoprenoid precursors into longer polyprenyl-PP groups required for diverse cellular processes such as protein prenylation and dolichol synthesis (Gisselberg et al., 2018; Gabriel et al., 2015a; No et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Gisselberg et al., 2018; Gabriel et al., 2015a; No et al., 2012).

claim: Known prenyltransferases in P. falciparum are cytoplasmic.
source: In addition, known prenyltransferases, which attach prenyl groups such as farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) and geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP) to client proteins, are also cytoplasmic (Imlay and Odom, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Imlay and Odom, 2014).

claim: FOS treatment of synchronized ring-stage parasites results in multinuclear schizonts with focal, unbranched apicoplast morphology.
source: Consistent with prior reports (Nair et al., 2011; Bowman et al., 2014; Goodman and McFadden, 2014; Howe et al., 2013), we observed that synchronized ring-stage parasites treated with FOS developed into multinuclear schizonts but failed to elongate the apicoplast, which retained a focal, unbranched morphology in PfMev (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and D10 parasites (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citations to prior work (Nair et al., 2011; Bowman et al., 2014; Goodman and McFadden, 2014; Howe et al., 2013).

claim: Parasites treated with lethal doses of drugs targeting processes outside the apicoplast exhibit normal apicoplast biogenesis.
source: In contrast to FOS treatment, parasites treated with lethal doses (10–100× EC50) of drugs that target processes outside the apicoplast, including DSM1 (mitochondrial dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibitor) (Phillips et al., 2008), atovaquone (ATV, mitochondrial cytochrome b inhibitor) (Fry and Pudney, 1992), blasticidin-S (Blast-S, cytoplasmic translation inhibitor) (Mamoun et al., 1999), or WR99210 (WR, cytoplasmic dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor) (Fidock and Wellems, 1997), exhibited normal apicoplast biogenesis as they developed into schizonts, very similar to untreated parasites (Figure 1B and C, and Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citations to prior work (Phillips et al., 2008; Fry and Pudney, 1992; Mamoun et al., 1999; Fidock and Wellems, 1997).

claim: Defects in apicoplast elongation observed with FOS treatment are due to specific inhibition of MEP pathway activity rather than non-specific effects of parasite death.
source: These observations strongly suggest that defects in apicoplast elongation observed with FOS treatment are due to specific inhibition of MEP pathway activity rather than non-specific, secondary effects of parasite death.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations comparing FOS to other lethal drugs.

claim: Simultaneous treatment with FOS and IPP rescues apicoplast elongation and branching.
source: To directly test this conclusion, we simultaneously treated synchronized rings with 10 µM FOS and either 200 µM IPP or 50 µM mevalonate (for PfMev parasites) and observed normal apicoplast elongation and branching in schizonts (Figure 1A and B, and Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3), consistent with a prior report (Bowman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citation to prior work (Bowman et al., 2014).

claim: Washing out mevalonate from ring-stage ΔDXs parasites results in multinuclear schizonts with focal, unbranched apicoplast morphologies.
source: In the presence of 50 µM mevalonate, ∆DXS parasites displayed normal apicoplast elongation and branching in schizonts. However, washing out mevalonate from ring-stage ∆DXS parasites to ablate IPP synthesis resulted in multinuclear schizonts with focal, unbranched apicoplast morphologies identical to those observed in the presence of FOS (Figure 1D and E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Apicoplast elongation and branching require IPP synthesis.
source: These results strongly support the conclusion that apicoplast elongation and branching require IPP synthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations with FOS and ΔDXs parasites.

claim: Delayed mevalonate supplementation can rescue parasite viability without rescuing apicoplast biogenesis.
source: We therefore reasoned that if IPP supplementation were delayed until mid-schizogony, after the onset of apicoplast-elongation defects but before broader cellular death, it might be possible to rescue parasite viability without rescuing apicoplast biogenesis and thereby produce viable parasite progeny that lacked the intact apicoplast.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by the delayed mevalonate rescue experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: A fraction of clonal parasites derived from delayed mevalonate rescue showed clear signs of apicoplast loss.
source: Although FOS-treated parasites supplemented simultaneously with mevalonate showed no evidence for apicoplast loss in clonal progeny, a fraction of clonal parasites derived from delayed mevalonate rescue showed clear signs of apicoplast loss, including a dispersed apicoplast ACPL-GFP signal, loss of the apicoplast genome, and growth dependence on exogenous mevalonate (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The fraction of clonal parasites with a disrupted apicoplast increased from 10% at 30 hr mevalonate supplementation to over 80% at 38 hr supplementation.
source: The fraction of clonal parasites with a disrupted apicoplast increased from 10% in parasites supplemented with mevalonate at 30 hr to over 80% in parasites supplemented at 38 hr (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Inhibiting IPP synthesis alone is sufficient to block apicoplast biogenesis and prevent organelle inheritance by daughter parasites.
source: These results provide direct evidence that inhibiting IPP synthesis alone is sufficient to block apicoplast biogenesis and prevent organelle inheritance by daughter parasites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the delayed mevalonate rescue experiments.

claim: MiaA is the only predicted isoprenoid-dependent metabolic pathway in the apicoplast.
source: Currently, the only predicted isoprenoid-dependent metabolic pathway in the apicoplast is tRNA prenylation by MiaA (Ralph et al., 2004; Imlay and Odom, 2014), which catalyzes the attachment of a dimethylallyl group to the N6 moiety of adenine at position 37 of certain tRNAs (Persson et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Ralph et al., 2004; Imlay and Odom, 2014; Persson et al., 1994).

claim: MiaA and MiaB are predicted to be non-essential for blood-stage Plasmodium based on genome-wide knockout studies.
source: Although genes encoding MiaA (PF3D7_1207600) and MiaB (PF3D7_0622200) are annotated in the P. falciparum genome and MiaA protein has been detected by mass spectrometry (MS) in the apicoplast-specific proteome (Boucher et al., 2018), neither protein has been studied biochemically in parasites. Nevertheless, both proteins are predicted to be non-essential for blood-stage Plasmodium based on genome-wide knockout (KO) studies in Plasmodium berghei (Bushell et al., 2017) and P. falciparum (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Boucher et al., 2018; Bushell et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018).

claim: ΔMiaA parasites grow equally well in the presence or absence of mevalonate.
source: The ∆MiaA parasites grew equally well in the presence or absence of mevalonate and grew indistinguishably from the parental PfMev parasites (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ΔMiaA parasites retain an intact apicoplast.
source: The presence of an intact apicoplast was confirmed by genomic PCR analysis and live parasite microscopy (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MiaA is dispensable for blood-stage parasites.
source: These results indicate that MiaA is dispensable for blood-stage parasites and that deletion of this gene does not affect apicoplast biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ΔMiaA experimental data.

claim: 5 µM GGOH but not FOH partially rescues parasite growth from inhibition by FOS.
source: Consistent with prior reports, 5 µM GGOH but not FOH partially rescued parasite growth from inhibition by FOS and enabled culture expansion into a second growth cycle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both GGOH and FOH rescue apicoplast elongation and branching defects when added simultaneously with FOS.
source: Nevertheless, both GGOH and FOH rescued apicoplast elongation and branching defects in schizonts when added simultaneously with FOS to synchronized rings (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: 5 µM decaprenol rescues apicoplast branching from FOS-induced defects.
source: We extended these rescue experiments to include 5 µM decaprenol (50 carbons) and also observed rescue of apicoplast branching from FOS-induced defects.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: 5 µM β-carotene does not rescue apicoplast biogenesis from inhibition by FOS.
source: However, 5 µM β-carotene, which is a nonlinear carotenoid hydrocarbon derived from eight prenyl groups (40 carbons), did not rescue apicoplast biogenesis from inhibition by FOS (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Apicoplast biogenesis specifically requires synthesis of linear polyprenols containing three or more prenyl groups.
source: Although it is possible that β-carotene is not taken up efficiently into the apicoplast, rescue by decaprenol, which is similar in size and hydrophobicity to β-carotene, suggests that apicoplast biogenesis specifically requires synthesis of linear polyprenols containing three or more prenyl groups.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential rescue by decaprenol versus β-carotene.

claim: PF3D7_0202700 shares 23% sequence identity with avian FPPS.
source: Therefore, we turned our attention to the second isoprenoid synthase homolog in P. falciparum, PF3D7_0202700, which shares 23% sequence identity with avian FPPS.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis described in the methods.

claim: PF3D7_0202700 retains the DDXXD sequence dyad expected for a polyprenyl pyrophosphate synthase.
source: Like the FPP/GGPP synthase, PF3D7_0202700 retains the DDXXD sequence dyad expected for a polyprenyl pyrophosphate synthase.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The amino acid floor of PF3D7_0202700 features a Gly-Ser dyad upstream of the first DDXXD, suggesting an ability to synthesize longer-chain isoprenoids greater than four isoprene units.
source: In addition, the amino acid floor of PF3D7_0202700 features a sterically smaller Gly-Ser dyad upstream of the first DDXXD (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) that suggests an ability to synthesize longer-chain isoprenoids greater than four isoprene units.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and structural modeling shown in Figure 5.

claim: A prior in vitro study reported that PF3D7_0202700 can synthesize polyprenyl-PP products of 8–11 isoprene units.
source: A prior in vitro study of PF3D7_0202700 function, using truncated recombinant protein expressed in E. coli or impure parasite extracts, reported an ability to synthesize polyprenyl-PP products of 8–11 isoprene units (Tonhosolo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Tonhosolo et al., 2005).

claim: PF3D7_0202700 localizes to the apicoplast based on co-localization with apicoplast ACP.
source: In live parasites, focal PPS-GFP fluorescence was detected in a tubular compartment proximal to but distinct from the mitochondrion, as expected for apicoplast localization. Immunofluorescence analysis (IFA) of the PPS-RFP line revealed strong co-localization between PPS-RFP and the apicoplast ACP (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PPS-GFP signal displays a constellation of dispersed fluorescent foci in parasites with disrupted apicoplasts.
source: As expected for an apicoplast-targeted protein, the PPS-GFP signal in these parasites displayed a constellation of dispersed fluorescent foci, rather than the concentrated signal observed in untreated parasites (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Western blot analysis of PPS-RFP parasites reveals two bands at the expected sizes for precursor protein and a smaller, N-terminally processed mature form.
source: Western blot analysis of the PPS-RFP parasites revealed two bands at the expected sizes for precursor protein and a smaller, N-terminally processed mature form, as expected for import into the apicoplast (Figure 5E; Waller et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and citation to prior work (Waller et al., 2000).

claim: In apicoplast-disrupted parasites, only a single PPS-RFP band for the precursor protein is detected.
source: In the apicoplast-disrupted parasites, however, only a single PPS-RFP band for the precursor protein was detected, consistent with loss of apicoplast import and lack of transit peptide removal (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Dahl et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and citations to prior work (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Dahl et al., 2006).

claim: PF3D7_0202700 is an apicoplast-targeted PPS that is imported into the organelle and N-terminally processed to a mature form.
source: On the basis of these observations, we conclude that PF3D7_0202700 is an apicoplast-targeted PPS that is imported into the organelle and N-terminally processed to a mature form.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the localization and western blot experiments.

claim: The genomic locus for PF3D7_0202700 was reported to be refractory to disruption in genome-wide KO studies.
source: The genomic locus for PF3D7_0202700 was reported to be refractory to disruption in recent genome-wide KO studies in P. berghei (Bushell et al., 2017) and P. falciparum, (Zhang et al., 2018) suggesting an essential function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Bushell et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018).

claim: Endogenous PPS co-localizes with apicoplast ACP.
source: We then used immunofluorescence microscopy to confirm co-localization of the endogenous PPS with apicoplast ACP (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Expression of the ~60 kDa HA-FLAG-tagged, endogenous mature PPS protein is reduced nearly threefold in parasites grown in -aTc + IPP conditions.
source: Expression of the ~60 kDa HA-FLAG-tagged, endogenous mature protein was detected by anti-HA-tag western blot in +aTc conditions, and its signal relative to the loading control was reduced nearly threefold in parasites grown in -aTc + IPP conditions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PPS transcript levels are robustly knocked down by the second intraerythrocytic cycle of parasite growth in -aTc conditions.
source: We also quantified PPS transcript levels by RT-qPCR and observed robust KD of PPS mRNA levels by the second intraerythrocytic cycle of parasite growth in -aTc conditions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PPS KD parasites show a major growth defect in the fourth cycle without aTc.
source: Without aTc, however, the culture grew normally over the first three intraerythrocytic cycles but showed a major growth defect in the fourth cycle consistent with extensive parasite death observed by blood smear (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Parasite growth under -aTc conditions is strongly rescued by 200 µM exogenous IPP.
source: Parasite growth under -aTc conditions was strongly rescued in the presence of 200 µM exogenous IPP (Figure 6E), indicating an essential PPS function specific to the apicoplast.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Only decaprenol, but not FOH or GGOH, rescues parasite growth in -aTc conditions.
source: We observed that only decaprenol, but not FOH or GGOH, rescued parasite growth in -aTc conditions, and the magnitude of rescue by decaprenol was comparable to IPP (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PPS has an essential function downstream of IPP synthesis in converting isoprenoid precursors into longer-chain linear polyprenyl-PPs containing at least 5–10 isoprene units.
source: These observations strongly suggest that PPS has an essential function downstream of IPP synthesis in converting isoprenoid precursors into longer-chain linear polyprenyl-PPs containing at least 5–10 isoprene units.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the selective rescue by decaprenol.

claim: ~30% of parasites cultured in -aTc conditions have a dispersed ACP signal indicative of apicoplast disruption.
source: IFA revealed that ~30% of parasites cultured in -aTc conditions had a dispersed ACP signal indicative of apicoplast disruption (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The vast majority (>80%) of -aTc parasites treated with FOS and IPP show focal, unbranched apicoplast morphology.
source: We observed normal apicoplast elongation in +aTc parasites but focal, unbranched apicoplast morphology in the vast majority (>80%) of -aTc parasites (Figure 7B and C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Substitution of IPP with FOH or GGOH results in a nearly identical apicoplast elongation defect in -aTc parasites.
source: Substitution of IPP with FOH or GGOH resulted in a nearly identical apicoplast elongation defect in -aTc parasites.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Substituting IPP with decaprenol results in normal apicoplast elongation in both +aTc and -aTc parasites.
source: In contrast, substituting IPP with decaprenol resulted in normal apicoplast elongation in both +aTc and -aTc parasites (Figure 7B and C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: The selective ability of decaprenol to rescue apicoplast-branching defects in -aTc conditions strongly supports an essential role for PPS in synthesizing long-chain polyprenyl isoprenoids required for apicoplast biogenesis.
source: The selective ability of decaprenol to rescue apicoplast-branching defects in -aTc conditions strongly supports an essential role for PPS in synthesizing long-chain polyprenyl isoprenoids required for apicoplast biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: The -aTc (+FOS and IPP) culture predominantly contains parasites with a dispersed ACP signal indicative of apicoplast loss after five 48 hr cycles.
source: Parasites cultured +aTc displayed normal elongated apicoplast morphology. In contrast, the -aTc (+FOS and IPP) culture predominantly contained parasites with a dispersed ACP signal indicative of apicoplast loss (Figure 7D and E, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: -aTc parasites contain a strongly reduced qPCR signal for apicoplast genomic DNA, relative to +aTc parasites.
source: These -aTc parasites also contained a strongly reduced qPCR signal for apicoplast genomic DNA, relative to +aTc parasites (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: PPS is essential for apicoplast maintenance and inheritance by daughter parasites.
source: These results indicate that PPS is essential for apicoplast maintenance and inheritance by daughter parasites such that loss of PPS function (with IPP supplementation) results in parasite progeny lacking the intact organelle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PPS KD experiments.

claim: Loss of PPS function is sufficient to explain the observation that blocking MEP pathway activity by FOS or ΔDXs inhibits apicoplast biogenesis.
source: This essential PPS function downstream of IPP synthesis by the MEP pathway is sufficient to explain our observation that blocking pathway activity by FOS or ∆DXS inhibits apicoplast biogenesis (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the PPS KD results to the earlier FOS and ΔDXs observations.

claim: There is no known enzyme that is capable of catalyzing both head-to-tail and head-to-head condensation of isoprenoids.
source: Given the mechanistic differences between head-to-tail and head-to-head condensation of isoprenoids (Figure 8A), which involve distinct positioning of substrate pyrophosphate groups within each active site, there is no known enzyme that is capable of catalyzing both reactions (Bouvier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Bouvier et al., 2005).

claim: Untargeted sequence similarity searches with PF3D7_0202700 as the query sequence only identify PPS homologs from bacteria, algae, and plants and fail to identify PSY homologs.
source: As noted previously, untargeted sequence similarity searches via NCBI BLAST (Boratyn et al., 2013) and MPI HHpred (Zimmermann et al., 2018) with PF3D7_0202700 as the query sequence only identify PPS homologs from bacteria, algae, and plants (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) and fail to identify PSY homologs.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis described in the methods.

claim: Targeted pairwise alignments show no evidence of significant sequence homology between PF3D7_0202700 and confirmed eukaryotic or prokaryotic PSY sequences.
source: Furthermore, targeted pairwise alignments show no evidence of significant sequence homology between PF3D7_0202700 and confirmed eukaryotic or prokaryotic PSY sequences from Arabidopsis thaliana (Uniprot P37271, chloroplast-targeted) (Zhou et al., 2015) or Erwinia herbicola (Pantoea agglomerans, Uniprot D5KXJ0) (Iwata-Reuyl et al., 2003), respectively.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and citations to prior work (Zhou et al., 2015; Iwata-Reuyl et al., 2003).

claim: The functional annotation of a bacterial protein (BAA94032) with sequence similarity to PF3D7_0202700 was revised from PSY to GGPPS.
source: We noted that the functional annotation of this bacterial protein was subsequently revised to a GGPPS (Uniprot I0HUM5) (Nagashima et al., 2012), thus explaining its sequence similarity to PF3D7_0202700 and the homology of both proteins to known PPSs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Nagashima et al., 2012).

claim: Zaragozic acid (ZA) inhibits blood-stage P. falciparum growth with an EC50 of ~10 µM in Dd2 parasites.
source: We repeated these experiments in Dd2 parasites and observed a similar EC50 of ~10 µM for ZA that increased fivefold to ~50 µM in Dd2 parasites episomally expressing PPS-RFP (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lethal growth inhibition by ZA is not rescued by exogenous IPP.
source: However, in contrast to PPS KD (Figure 6D), lethal growth inhibition by ZA was not rescued by exogenous IPP (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and did not affect apicoplast elongation (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: PPS and the apicoplast are not uniquely targeted by ZA.
source: These contrasting phenotypes strongly suggest that PPS, and more broadly the apicoplast, are not uniquely targeted by ZA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the contrasting phenotypes of ZA versus PPS KD.

claim: PPS KD parasites grown ±aTc have indistinguishable low levels of β-carotene.
source: We observed indistinguishable low levels of β-carotene in both samples (Figure 8B), providing no evidence that PPS plays a role in carotenoid biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Extracts of uninfected erythrocytes incubated in complete RPMI medium containing AlbuMAX have β-carotene levels nearly identical to extracts of parasite-infected erythrocytes.
source: Although uninfected erythrocytes washed in AlbuMAX-free RPMI lacked detectable β-carotene, we observed that extracts of uninfected erythrocytes incubated in complete RPMI medium containing AlbuMAX I had β-carotene levels that were nearly identical to extracts of parasite-infected erythrocytes (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: AlbuMAX contains modest levels of β-carotene.
source: Analysis of AlbuMAX (Thermo Fisher catalog #11020021) by MS revealed modest levels of β-carotene (Figure 8—figure supplement 4), consistent with the bovine origin of AlbuMAX (lipid-rich bovine serum albumin) and the plant-based diet of these animals expected to contain β-carotene.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: There is no evidence that PPS function contributes to β-carotene levels in P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes.
source: In summary, we find no evidence that PPS function contributes to β-carotene levels in P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes, which we suggest non-specifically take up exogenous plant-derived β-carotene associated with AlbuMAX in the culture medium.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the β-carotene analysis experiments.

claim: Unlabeled β-carotene (m/z 536.4) is readily detected in PfMev parasites cultured in 2-13C-mevalonate and FOS.
source: Although we readily detected unlabeled β-carotene (m/z 536.4), which we attribute to culture medium AlbuMAX, we were unable to detect 13C-labeled β-carotene (m/z 544.4) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: 13C-labeled β-carotene (m/z 544.4) is not detected in PfMev parasites cultured in 2-13C-mevalonate and FOS.
source: Although we readily detected unlabeled β-carotene (m/z 536.4), which we attribute to culture medium AlbuMAX, we were unable to detect 13C-labeled β-carotene (m/z 544.4) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Fully 13C-labeled β-carotene (m/z 576.6) is readily detected in E. coli bacteria engineered to biosynthesize β-carotene and grown in uniformly labeled 13C-glucose.
source: In contrast to the parasite analysis, we readily detected fully 13C-labeled β-carotene (m/z 576.6) produced by E. coli bacteria engineered to biosynthesize β-carotene (Cunningham and Gantt, 2005) and grown in minimal M9 medium with uniformly labeled 13C-glucose as the sole carbon source (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D and citation to prior work (Cunningham and Gantt, 2005).

claim: There is no evidence for PSY function by PF3D7_0202700 or for de novo carotenoid synthesis by blood-stage P. falciparum parasites.
source: In summary, we find no evidence for PSY function by PF3D7_0202700 or for de novo carotenoid synthesis by blood-stage P. falciparum parasites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the isotope labeling and β-carotene analysis experiments.

claim: PF3D7_0202700 functions exclusively as a PPS required for apicoplast biogenesis.
source: Collectively, our data strongly support the conclusion that PF3D7_0202700 functions exclusively as a PPS required for apicoplast biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental data on PPS function.

claim: This discovery expands the paradigm for isoprenoid utilization in P. falciparum.
source: This discovery critically expands the paradigm for isoprenoid utilization in P. falciparum, identifies a potential new apicoplast drug target, and uncovers an organelle maintenance pathway whose inhibition causes first-cycle defects in apicoplast inheritance in contrast to delayed death-inducing antibiotics.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the significance of the findings.

claim: PPS is a potential new apicoplast drug target.
source: This discovery critically expands the paradigm for isoprenoid utilization in P. falciparum, identifies a potential new apicoplast drug target, and uncovers an organelle maintenance pathway whose inhibition causes first-cycle defects in apicoplast inheritance in contrast to delayed death-inducing antibiotics.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the therapeutic potential of the findings.

claim: Inhibition of PPS causes first-cycle defects in apicoplast inheritance in contrast to delayed death-inducing antibiotics.
source: This discovery critically expands the paradigm for isoprenoid utilization in P. falciparum, identifies a potential new apicoplast drug target, and uncovers an organelle maintenance pathway whose inhibition causes first-cycle defects in apicoplast inheritance in contrast to delayed death-inducing antibiotics.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing growth defects in the fourth cycle of PPS KD.

claim: IPP synthesis by the MEP pathway requires apicoplast maintenance.
source: Prior work has clearly established that apicoplast maintenance pathways are required to support IPP synthesis and export for essential cellular use (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Kennedy et al., 2019a; Gisselberg et al., 2013; Dahl et al., 2006), but the reverse dependence of apicoplast biogenesis on IPP was not previously recognized.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Kennedy et al., 2019a; Gisselberg et al., 2013; Dahl et al., 2006).

claim: Apicoplast biogenesis depends on IPP synthesis.
source: Prior work has clearly established that apicoplast maintenance pathways are required to support IPP synthesis and export for essential cellular use (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011; Kennedy et al., 2019a; Gisselberg et al., 2013; Dahl et al., 2006), but the reverse dependence of apicoplast biogenesis on IPP was not previously recognized.
evidence: This is a key finding of the current study.

claim: IPP synthesis by the MEP pathway and apicoplast maintenance are convoluted and interdependent.
source: Thus, IPP synthesis by the MEP pathway requires apicoplast maintenance, which in turn depends on IPP synthesis. The two processes are convoluted and interdependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: Inhibition of apicoplast maintenance pathways can kill parasites with first-cycle kinetics.
source: Our results also support the emerging paradigm (Uddin et al., 2018; Amberg-Johnson et al., 2017; Boucher and Yeh, 2019; Okada et al., 2020) that inhibition of apicoplast maintenance pathways can kill parasites with first-cycle kinetics that defy the delayed-death phenotype commonly observed for translation-blocking antibiotics such as doxycycline that target organelle housekeeping (Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007; Uddin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Uddin et al., 2018; Amberg-Johnson et al., 2017; Boucher and Yeh, 2019; Okada et al., 2020; Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007).

claim: Blocking IPP synthesis causes same-cycle defects in apicoplast biogenesis.
source: Indeed, blocking IPP synthesis causes same-cycle defects in apicoplast biogenesis, which are expected to produce non-viable parasite progeny independent of lethal dysfunctions in isoprenoid-dependent metabolism outside the organelle.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The critical role of IPP for apicoplast biogenesis precedes the broader cellular need for IPP outside the organelle in mature schizonts.
source: Thus, the critical role of IPP for apicoplast biogenesis precedes the broader cellular need for IPP outside the organelle in mature schizonts, suggested by recent works to predominantly reflect essential roles for IPP-dependent protein prenylation (Kennedy et al., 2019a; Howe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing of FOS-induced defects and citations to prior work (Kennedy et al., 2019a; Howe et al., 2013).

claim: IPP utilization in the apicoplast depends on de novo synthesis rather than a pre-existing metabolite pool.
source: This observation suggests that IPP utilization in the apicoplast depends on de novo synthesis rather than a pre-existing metabolite pool, possibly because IPP does not accumulate in the apicoplast and/or that IPP synthesis within the organelle is differentially partitioned for export and internal utilization.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation that FOS inhibits apicoplast elongation regardless of when it is added.

claim: N-terminal processing of apicoplast-targeted proteins is an exclusive property of known proteins imported into the organelle.
source: N-terminal processing of apicoplast-targeted proteins is an exclusive property of known proteins imported into the organelle.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Multiple proteins that associate with the apicoplast exterior or target the outer apicoplast membrane are not N-terminally processed.
source: Although multiple proteins have been shown or suggested to associate with the apicoplast exterior or target the outer apicoplast membrane, none of these proteins is N-terminally processed (e.g., ATG8, oTPT, and FTSH1) (Amberg-Johnson et al., 2017; Mullin et al., 2006; Tomlins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Amberg-Johnson et al., 2017; Mullin et al., 2006; Tomlins et al., 2013).

claim: N-terminal processing of PPS is strongly suggestive of import into the apicoplast.
source: N-terminal processing of PPS is therefore strongly suggestive of import into the apicoplast.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the established knowledge about N-terminal processing.

claim: The reliance of apicoplast biogenesis on isoprenoid synthesis in Plasmodium may differ from other apicomplexan parasites.
source: The reliance of apicoplast biogenesis on isoprenoid synthesis in Plasmodium may differ from other apicomplexan parasites.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the discussion of differences between Plasmodium and Toxoplasma.

claim: Loss of MEP pathway activity in T. gondii does not impact apicoplast biogenesis.
source: Furthermore, a recent study (Henkel et al., 2022) showed that loss of MEP pathway activity in T. gondii (due to loss of apicoplast ferredoxin) does not impact apicoplast biogenesis, in contrast to our observations in P. falciparum based on FOS treatment, DXS deletion, and PPS KD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Henkel et al., 2022).

claim: Linear polyprenyl alcohols are important components of plant membranes, especially chloroplast membranes.
source: Linear polyprenyl alcohols have been found to be important components of plant membranes, especially chloroplast membranes, where they are proposed to modulate membrane structure, fluidity, and dynamics (Akhtar et al., 2017; Van Gelder et al., 2018; Hartley and Imperiali, 2012; Swiezewska and Danikiewicz, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Akhtar et al., 2017; Van Gelder et al., 2018; Hartley and Imperiali, 2012; Swiezewska and Danikiewicz, 2005).

claim: Linear polyprenols or polyprenyl phosphates may serve as critical components of the apicoplast membranes and be required for maintaining membrane fluidity during organelle biogenesis.
source: In the absence of other known roles for longer-chain polyprenyl-PPs in the apicoplast, we hypothesize that linear polyprenols or polyprenyl phosphates may serve as critical components of the apicoplast membranes and be required for maintaining membrane fluidity during organelle biogenesis (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations and knowledge from plant biology.

claim: PPS function is critical for parasite survival.
source: Independent of its specific role in apicoplast biogenesis, PPS function is critical for parasite survival and thus constitutes a new essential arm of isoprenoid metabolism in the apicoplast suitable for development as a therapeutic target.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing lethality of PPS KD.

claim: The substantial sequence differences between PPS and human orthologs will facilitate selective targeting of PPS by chemical inhibitors.
source: The substantial sequence differences with human orthologs will facilitate selective targeting of PPS by chemical inhibitors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the therapeutic potential based on sequence analysis.

claim: New metabolic pathways and functions remain to be discovered and/or localized to the apicoplast.
source: Identification of PPS as an apicoplast-targeted enzyme indicates that new metabolic pathways and functions remain to be discovered and/or localized to the apicoplast.
evidence: This is a general statement about the implications of the findings.
